endorsements.quote: At the design phase, the interdisciplinary AI development team (see glossary) should identify possible types and sources of bias for their AI tool.

Furthermore, relevant information about the datasets, such as the centres where they were acquired, the machine used, the preprocessing and annotation processes, should be systematically collected to address technical and human biases.

When possible—that is, the individuals’ and data attributes are available—bias detection methods should be applied by using fairness metrics such as true positive rates, statistical parity, group fairness, and equalised odds.

To correct for any identified biases, mitigation measures should be tested, such as data resampling, bias free representations, and equalised odds postprocessing, 36 37 38 39 40 to verify their impact on both the tool’s fairness and the model’s accuracy.
Importantly, any remaining bias should be documented and reported to inform the end users and citizens (see traceability 2).
To assess generalisability, technical validation of the AI tools should be performed with external datasets that are distinct from those used for model training.
The AI tool should be evaluated for its clinical utility and safety.
Additionally, it is important to show that the AI tool is safe and does not cause harm to individuals (or specific groups), such as through a randomised clinical trial.

Throughout the AI tool’s lifecycle, the multidisciplinary development team shall analyse potential risks, assess each risk’s likelihood, effects and risk-benefit balance, define risk mitigation measures, monitor the risks and mitigations continuously, and maintain a risk management file.

To increase transparency, traceability, and accountability, adequate documentation should be created and maintained for the AI tool, 48 which might include (a) an AI information leaflet to inform citizens and healthcare professionals about the tool’s intended use, risks (eg, biases) and instructions for use; (b) a technical document to inform AI developers, health organisations, and regulators about the AI model’s properties (eg, hyperparameters), training and testing data, evaluation criteria and results, biases and other limitations, and periodic audits and updates 49 50 51 ; (c) a publication based on existing AI reporting standards 13 15 52 ; and (d) a risk management file (see traceability 1).

The AI tool should be developed and deployed with mechanisms for continuous monitoring and quality control of the AI inputs and outputs, 47 such as to identify missing or out-of-range input variables, inconsistent data formats or units, incorrect annotations or data preprocessing, and erroneous or implausible AI outputs.
For quality control of the AI decisions, uncertainty estimates should be provided (and calibrated 53 ) to inform the end users about the degree of confidence in the results.
The AI tool should be developed and deployed with a configurable system for periodic auditing, 47 which should define the datasets and timelines for periodic evaluations (eg, every year).
The periodic auditing should enable the identification of data or concept drifts, newly occurring biases, performance degradation or changes in the decision making of the end users.

To increase traceability and accountability, an AI logging system should be implemented to trace the user’s main actions in a privacy preserving manner, specify the data that are accessed and used, record the AI predictions and clinical decisions, and log any encountered issues.
In particular, the roles of risk management, periodic auditing, maintenance, and supervision should be assigned, such as to IT teams or healthcare administrators.
Furthermore, responsibilities for AI related errors should be clearly specified among clinicians, healthcare centres, AI developers, and manufacturers.

Usability 4: Evaluate clinical usability To facilitate adoption, the usability of the AI tool within the local clinical workflows should be evaluated in real world settings with representative and diverse end users (eg, with respect to sex, gender, age, clinical role, digital proficiency, and disability).
Evaluation studies should be implemented to evaluate the AI tool’s robustness (eg, stress tests, repeatability tests 62 ) under conditions that reflect the variations of real world clinical practice.

The explainable AI methods should be evaluated, first quantitatively by using computational methods to assess the correctness of the explanations, 70 71 then qualitatively with end users to assess their impact on user satisfaction, confidence, and clinical performance.

If so, the specific requirements for explainability should be defined with representative experts and end users, including (a) the goal of the explanations (eg, global description of the model’s behaviour v local explanation of each AI decision); (b) the most suitable approach for AI explainability 69 ; and (c) the potential limitations to anticipate and monitor (eg, over-reliance of the end users on the AI decision 68 ).
The development team should identify the applicable AI regulations, which vary by jurisdiction and over time.

In addition to the well known ethical issues that arise in medical AI (eg, privacy, transparency, equity, autonomy), AI developers, domain specialists, and professional ethicists should identify, discuss, and address all application specific ethical, social, and societal issues as an integral part of the development and deployment of the AI tool.
In particular, the test data should be well separated from the training to prevent data leakage.
Finally, benchmarking with respect to reference AI tools or standard practice should be performed to enable comparative assessment of model performance.
Furthermore, adequate evaluation metrics should be carefully selected, taking into account their benefits and potential flaws.

Furthermore, the manufacturers and deployers should implement and regularly evaluate measures for protecting the AI tool against malicious or adversarial attacks, such as by using system level cybersecurity solutions or application specific defence mechanisms (eg, attack detection or mitigation).
If the performance is decreased when evaluated locally, recalibration of the AI model should be performed and tested (eg, through model fine tuning).
Therefore, the training datasets should be carefully selected, analysed, and enriched according to the sources of variation identified at the design phase (see robustness 1).

unlisted_practices: Developers should define intended clinical settings and anticipate cross-setting variations before development.
Developers should build AI tools on existing community-defined standards such as clinical definitions, medical ontologies, data models, and interface standards.
Developers should define human-in-the-loop mechanisms enabling users to verify AI results and overrule AI predictions.
Developers should provide training materials and activities in accessible formats and languages for diverse end users.
Developers should engage interdisciplinary stakeholders continuously throughout the AI lifecycle.
Developers should implement privacy-enhancing measures and data protection impact assessment for AI tools throughout the lifecycle.
Developers should define robustness requirements by inventorying real-world sources of data variation at the design phase.
Developers should apply and test mitigation measures such as transfer learning or domain adaptation when generalisability is limited.
Developers should engage clinical experts and end users early to define intended use and user requirements, including human factors such as automation bias.
Developers should consider strategies to reduce the carbon footprint of AI tools.

screen.reason: This is an international consensus guideline and framework paper (FUTURE-AI) outlining recommendations and best practices for trustworthy and deployable AI in healthcare.
